California EV Demand After Two Market Shocks

Tax-credit expiration, fuel pressure, and the 2026 rebound

MSBA 580 Project Group

July 2026

Executive report

Decision question

California EV manufacturers, dealers, and marketing managers need to decide whether the early-2026 gasoline-price shock created a durable EV sales opportunity after the federal purchase credit expired in September 2025. We ask: Did California’s zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) market rebound as fuel pressure increased, and was the rebound large enough to offset the post-credit decline? We also examine whether Californians reduced driving and whether counties followed distinct response patterns.

California’s ZEV share recovered from its 2026 Q1 low, but by Q2 it was only 0.19 percentage points above the post-credit 2025 Q4 level. The rebound coincided with higher gasoline prices and EV search interest, but cannot prove causation. VMT provides mixed evidence of reduced driving. Managers should treat the period as renewed attention, not a permanent demand shift.

Data and analytical approach

The project combines independently sourced public data. California Energy Commission records provide quarterly new light-duty ZEV and total light-duty sales statewide and by county. ZEVs include battery electric, plug-in hybrid, and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles; they exclude used and medium- or heavy-duty vehicles. EIA data supply gasoline prices; Google Trends supplies relative interest, not search counts; and FHWA Traffic Volume Trends supplies monthly statewide VMT.

The observed-market analysis uses two major techniques. First, a pre-event regression benchmark fits a linear time trend and calendar-quarter indicators to 2023 Q1 through 2025 Q2, then compares later observations with predictions. We compare that specification with simpler alternatives using small-sample AICc and leave-one-out error and report robust and influence diagnostics.

Second, k-means segmentation groups the 58 California county mailing-address categories using standardized 2025 Q4 ZEV share, the change through 2026 Q2, and log average quarterly light-duty sales. We inspect two through six clusters using mean silhouette width and select three for parsimony and business interpretability. The silhouette near 0.34 indicates only moderate separation, so these are descriptive archetypes rather than permanent county types.

Third, a rating-based conjoint model analyzes 123 completed profile ratings from 18 respondents. Ratings are reversed so higher scores mean greater preference, then modeled with effect-coded attributes, respondent fixed effects, and respondent-clustered standard errors.

What changed?

ZEV share reached 28.3% in 2025 Q3 as purchases were likely pulled forward before the federal credit expired. It then fell 9.43 percentage points to 18.9% in 2025 Q4, a 33.3% relative decline, and fell again to 15.8% in 2026 Q1. The share rebounded 3.33 percentage points to 19.1% in 2026 Q2. Thus, the full post-war quarter recovered the first-quarter loss but did not meaningfully exceed the immediate post-credit baseline.

Observed statewide ZEV share and the pre-event time-plus-season benchmark.

The benchmark expected 22.5% in 2026 Q2, 3.38 points above observed, although the observation remained inside its 17.7%–27.3% prediction interval. With only 10 training quarters, one influential observation, and simpler models performing better on some criteria, this is a visualization—not a causal counterfactual.

Between 2025 Q4 and 2026 Q2, average California regular gasoline prices rose 32.0%, from $4.34 to $5.73 per gallon, and Google Trends interest in “electric vehicle” rose 140%. Attention clearly increased, but a normalized search index cannot measure the number or purchase intent of searchers.

Geographic and behavioral response

Forty-nine of 58 counties increased ZEV share, with a median increase of 2.35 percentage points. The official statewide result includes an “Out of State” mailing-address category; excluding that category raises the aggregate change from 0.19 to 1.27 percentage points. The official measure remains primary, and the county-only calculation is a sensitivity check.

County segment positions; point size represents average quarterly light-duty sales.

The 27 large established markets average a 2.03-point gain. The 16 low-adoption/stalled counties decline 0.36 points. Fifteen small markets average a 6.09-point rebound, but small denominators magnify movements.

VMT does not show a large sustained driving reduction. March, April, and May 2026 changed +3.5%, -0.8%, and -0.1% from the same months a year earlier. The three-month mean was +0.87%; May is preliminary and June was unavailable.

Monthly change from the same month one year earlier.

Stated preferences

The survey provides complementary stated-preference evidence. Price was the clearest attribute (cluster-robust p = 0.013): a $30,000 profile scored 1.30 points above a $120,000 profile (p = 0.005). Tesla was paired almost exclusively with 110 MPGe, so brand and fuel economy cannot be cleanly separated.

Rating-based conjoint part-worth utilities with respondent-clustered 95% intervals.

Managerial recommendations

Managers should not make a statewide inventory bet based on one post-war quarter. In large established EV markets, maintain inventory availability and use fuel-cost messaging to convert renewed search interest. In low-adoption counties, diagnose charging access, affordability, and awareness before adding inventory. In small fast-rebound markets, use light-touch campaigns and avoid overreacting to volatile percentage changes. The survey supports emphasizing affordability and total ownership cost, but not a brand-specific conclusion. Continue monthly leading-indicator tracking and re-estimate the benchmark when more quarters become available.

Limitations and next analysis

The study is observational and cannot separate the war, gasoline prices, tax policy, interest rates, manufacturer incentives, seasonality, and vehicle prices. County observations share the same statewide environment and are not independent replications of the shock. Google Trends is relative, VMT is incomplete for 2026 Q2, and the sales series has only one complete post-war quarter. The conjoint sample is small, uses ratings rather than forced choices, and has 17 missing ratings. Its brand–fuel-economy confounding prevents clean attribute separation, so we do not report willingness to pay or simulated choice shares.
